extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, federal judges, and law students studying patent trial practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on pleadings, demurrers, trial modes, evidence, expert testimony, and prima facie proof in U.S. patent infringement actions in federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of pleadings and effect of defective pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: The court will examine all pleadings and will generally decide against the party who first filed a substantially defective pleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal exception: a demurrer pointed at an entire declaration will not be sustained if some independent part of the declaration is good in law. This exception does not apply to demurrers to pleas, replications, or rejoinders, which are entire pleadings and if bad in part are bad for the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for demurrer to a declaration in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration is demurrable when the patent appears void on its face or by judicial notice; when the plaintiff omits necessary allegations; when allegations are in improper form; or when the statement of infringement covers a period, or part of a period, barred by statute of limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only part of the alleged infringement is time-barred, defendant should interpose a special demurrer aimed at that part; a general demurrer to whole declaration will be overruled if an independent divisible unbarred part remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for demurrer to a plea in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A plea is demurrable when the facts stated constitute no defense, are in improper form, or when the statute of limitations is pleaded to the whole of a right of action while only part is actually barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plea that is bad in part is bad altogether; demurrers to pleas differ from demurrers to declarations in their treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder in demurrer and procedural consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A joinder in demurrer is the proper response to a demurrer; actual filing of a written joinder is generally waived and demurrers are often brought for argument without that formality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a demurrer to an entire declaration is sustained on incurable grounds the plaintiff must file an exception and appeal or abandon action. If demurrer to a declaration is overruled, defendant may either appeal or obtain leave to file a plea but cannot later set up defenses that were in the overruled demurrer. Tactical advice: do not trust any vital defense solely to a demurrer unless no other vital defense exists or certainty of success exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible modes of trial
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent infringement action may be tried by jury, judge (bench), or by a referee, but jury trial is the only proper method absent consent to another mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may waive jury by written stipulation filed with the clerk. Trial by a court-appointed referee with consent of both parties is lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury size and unanimity requirements in federal patent trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial by jury must, absent contrary consent, be by a jury of twelve men; unanimity is necessary to a verdict of a federal jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State statutes permitting nonunanimous verdicts (e.g., three-fourths) do not apply in federal courts because of the Seventh Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local practice governs federal district courts sitting as law courts
rubrics_metrics.description: When sitting as law courts, each District Court is governed in matters of practice by the laws of the State in which it is established, so far as those laws are applicable, and by its own rules or customs where no state law exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District Courts may make and enforce their own rules of practice provided they are not repugnant to federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicable rules of evidence in patent trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of evidence in patent causes are the ordinary common-law rules, as modified by the statutes of the particular State and as adapted by U.S. court decisions to the circumstances of patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State statutory modifications and federal decisions shape admissibility and procedure in particular trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters patent as prima facie evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff's first item of evidence is the letters patent (or a certified copy authenticated by the Commissioner), which are prima facie evidence of validity unless the patent on its face does not conform to statutory form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption strengthened when alleged anticipating patent was considered by the Patent Office during prosecution; presumption weakened when similar prior references were not interposed or considered. Printed memorandum at head of specification stating filing date is not prima facie evidence of that date—prove by certified copy of the application when material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue patents as prima facie evidence (jurisdiction, breadth, identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reissue letters patent are prima facie evidence of their own validity with respect to (1) the Commissioner's jurisdiction to treat the original as proper subject for reissue, (2) facts bearing on broadened reissue after lapse of time, and (3) that the reissue does not claim a different invention than the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumptions are based on the Commissioner's assumed jurisdiction and knowledge of law; reissue is prima facie as to these three points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that patents appearing in full force are valid and unexpired
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters patent that appear on their face to be in full force are presumed to be so, and thus prima facie evidence that they have not been repealed by court decree nor expired by reason of the expiration of some foreign patent for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, certain defenses (e.g., nineteenth and twentieth defences referenced in text) need not be anticipated by plaintiff when introducing prima facie evidence of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of title to sue when plaintiff is not patentee
rubrics_metrics.description: After introducing the letters patent, if the plaintiff is not the patentee he must prove his title to the right sued upon—either that he was the assignee at the time of infringement or a grantee as to the relevant territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof may be by introducing original assignments/grants constituting chain of title; acknowledged documents carry prima facie proof via acknowledgment certificate; if no acknowledgment, prove according to common-law rules (produce subscribing witness, prove whereabouts, or prove genuineness of signature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of certified Patent Office copies of assignment records
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a certified copy of the Patent Office record of an assignment is admissible as evidence of the original has been ruled variously over time (affirmative and negative decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assuming negative decisions, inadmissibility may nevertheless be waived by omission to make a proper objection when such a copy is offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to prove absence of license; must prove marking or notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff is not required to prove in his prima facie evidence that defendant has no license or release, but must prove that plaintiff never made or sold specimens without statutory marking or that defendant was duly notified of infringement and continued after notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory marking requirements must be strictly complied with; when a patented device is part of a complete structure, marking must be on the patented device, or if not practicable, on package or label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of defendant's making/selling/using (nature and extent) as part of prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof that defendant made, sold, or used a specimen before the suit is the next step in proving a prima facie case; evidence must show both the nature and extent of the defendant's doings to support infringement and damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point often covered by stipulation. Courts of law cannot order inspections of defendant's works; defendant may be called as witness and compelled to describe actions; discovery of doings may be obtained via equity in aid of law action. If defendant cannot be relied upon, plaintiff must secure other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: When infringement is established (identity, estoppel, or immaterial differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of infringement is complete if defendant's doings are obviously and unquestionably identical with what is covered by the patent, or if defendant is estopped from denying identity; where differences exist, plaintiff may still prevail if differences are immaterial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court interprets patent terms in ordinary sense; often necessary to introduce expert testimony to show differences are immaterial and that defendant's actions constituted infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and admissibility of expert testimony in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts in patent cases are typically qualified by extensive theoretical and practical knowledge in mechanics, chemistry, electricity, or other relevant sciences; their opinions on relevant facts are admissible but should be accompanied by statements of good reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts may testify to experiments they made, but such testimony is weaker if opposing party couldn't observe experiments. Expert may prepare testimony in advance but cannot adopt another's written exposition as his own. Communications between experts and counsel are not privileged and may be inquired into on cross-examination to disclose origins of opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: How juries should weigh conflicting expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Juries should consider the experts' respective reasons, ability, knowledge, and fairness rather than their number or fame when deciding between contradictory expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience-based testimony generally has more weight than purely theoretical opinions; careful, studied views may be more nearly true than hurried opinions by more distinguished men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts may not testify to patent construction; court decides construction
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert cannot properly testify as to the construction of a patent (which is a question of law for the court), and a witness stating whether something infringes a patent is inadmissible because it includes a construction of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because construction is for the court, hypothetical questions embodying counsel's proposed constructions may be put to experts. If the court later gives a different construction, answers to hypotheticals inconsistent with it are immaterial. Counsel should use multiple hypothetical constructions if uncertain which will be adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible factual testimony by experts that affects construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Although experts cannot state legal construction, they may testify to facts that control construction (e.g., state of the art), similarities/differences in operation, whether parts perform same function and in substantially same way, and other factual matters relevant to infringement, invention, or abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construction depends on factual state of the art, the judge may instruct the jury conditionally ('if you find the state of the art to be X, then the patent is entitled to construction Y'). Generally questions of similarity/difference and other factual issues are for the jury and proper for expert testimony. Exception: where comparison of patents makes infringement solely a question of law for the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on cross-examination of expert witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expert expounds the prior art in his direct testimony, cross-examination may extend to those domains; but if the expert confines testimony to similarities and differences between plaintiff's patent and defendant's doings, cross-examination cannot generally extend to the prior art except to ask whether the expert considered it when forming his opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-examination may not probe matters irrelevant to the case or ask about characteristics unrelated to the issues merely to test knowledge or fairness; allowing such would introduce immaterial issues and distract the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of damages as part of prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: The final part of a plaintiff's prima facie evidence is proof of the amount of damages (sometimes supplemented by evidence supporting an award greater than actual damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The topic is extensive and treated separately; plaintiffs must present satisfactory proof of extent of infringement as an indispensable element of damages.
